subsystems.name: Algorithm specification
subsystems.role: the mathematical problem, written as something a quantum computer could run.
parts: block encoding of the Hamiltonian or oracle

subsystems.name: Error-correction model
subsystems.role: decides how logical qubits are protected and how they are laid out.

subsystems.name: Compilation and routing
subsystems.role: maps logical operations onto a two-dimensional grid of patches, cycle by cycle.

subsystems.name: Magic state factories
subsystems.role: produces the non-Clifford resource that usually dominates the cost.

subsystems.name: Hardware error model
subsystems.role: the assumed physical behaviour that everything else depends on.

subsystems.name: Cost accounting
subsystems.role: turns all of the above into the numbers people quote.

buildSteps.title: Fix the algorithmic target
buildSteps.detail: State the exact problem instance and the circuit that solves it — a chemistry Hamiltonian, a factoring instance, a differential-equation solver — including the precision required.

buildSteps.title: Choose the code and layout
buildSteps.detail: Pick an error-correcting code, almost always the surface code, and arrange the logical qubits as patches on a 2D grid with enough room for routing.

buildSteps.title: Set the failure budget
buildSteps.detail: Decide the acceptable chance the whole run fails, then split that budget across all logical operations and cycles so no step is allowed to dominate.

buildSteps.title: Solve for code distance
buildSteps.detail: Using the assumed physical error rate, raise the code distance until the logical error per cycle — which falls roughly exponentially in distance below threshold — meets the budget. This is the step where modest error-rate changes cause huge qubit-count changes.

buildSteps.title: Cost the Clifford operations
buildSteps.detail: Count surface-code cycles for each logical gate and for lattice surgery, add routing and idle time, and multiply by the cycle time to get the runtime floor.

buildSteps.title: Cost the non-Clifford resource
buildSteps.detail: Count the T gates, then size distillation or cultivation factories big enough to supply them at the pace the algorithm consumes them, and add those qubits to the footprint.

buildSteps.title: Total the machine
buildSteps.detail: Sum data qubits, factory qubits and routing overhead; take the critical path of the schedule as runtime; report physical qubits, hours, and the assumed error model together, because the numbers are meaningless apart.

buildSteps.title: Test sensitivity
buildSteps.detail: Re-run at several physical error rates and gate speeds to show how steeply the cost curves — the honest output is a range and a threshold, not a single number.

prerequisites.tech: Quantum error-correcting codes with proven thresholds
prerequisites.why: resource estimates are only meaningful if logical errors are known to shrink as code distance grows.

prerequisites.tech: Lattice surgery and logical gate schemes
prerequisites.why: they define the actual sequences of physical operations being counted.
non-Clifford gates are the dominant cost line in nearly every estimate.

prerequisites.tech: Measured hardware error rates and cycle times
prerequisites.why: estimates inherit the assumptions; today's devices are characterised, but the numbers drift and leakage and correlated errors are poorly bounded.

prerequisites.tech: Efficient block encodings for real problems
prerequisites.why: if the encoding is inefficient, the estimate reflects the encoding rather than the hardware.

prerequisites.tech: Automated estimator tooling tied to compilers
prerequisites.why: manual estimates take months and are hard to reproduce or compare.

pathway.milestone: published estimates for chemistry and for factoring 2048-bit RSA numbers, the latter landing at roughly twenty million physical qubits running for hours
pathway.unlocks: a shared, if pessimistic, yardstick for comparing algorithms and architectures.

pathway.milestone: hardware-aware estimates using measured error models, real device layouts, leakage and correlated-error data
pathway.unlocks: credible milestone planning instead of headline qubit counts.

pathway.milestone: estimators embedded in compilers so algorithm designers see cost while they write code
pathway.unlocks: algorithms redesigned for the hardware rather than translated onto it.

pathway.milestone: estimates validated against measured logical error rates on small demonstrations
pathway.unlocks: predictive engineering, where a paper's qubit count is a design commitment rather than a guess.

pathway.milestone: early fault-tolerant applications where the estimate decides which problem is attempted first
pathway.unlocks: a defensible answer to what a quantum computer is actually for.
